cmo-cmo-2012-01.title: Telescoping sum of squares
cmo-cmo-2012-01.body:
For every real $t$, $(t - 2)^2 \ge 0$, i.e. $t^2 \ge 4t - 4$. Apply this to $t = x, y, z$ and multiply the second and third inequalities by the positive numbers $x$ and $xy$:
$$x^2 \ge 4x - 4, \qquad xy^2 \ge 4xy - 4x, \qquad xyz^2 \ge 4xyz - 4xy.$$
Adding,
$$x^2 + xy^2 + xyz^2 \ge (4x - 4) + (4xy - 4x) + (4xyz - 4xy) = 4xyz - 4.$$
Equality holds exactly when $x = y = z = 2$. ∎

cmo-cmo-2012-01.title: Complete the squares directly
cmo-cmo-2012-01.body:
$$x^2 + xy^2 + xyz^2 - 4xyz + 4 = (x - 2)^2 + x(y - 2)^2 + xy(z - 2)^2,$$
as one checks by expanding the right side: $x^2 - 4x + 4 + xy^2 - 4xy + 4x + xyz^2 - 4xyz + 4xy$. Since $x, xy > 0$, each term is $\ge 0$, which proves the inequality. ∎

cmo-cmo-2012-02.title: Powers of a large prime
cmo-cmo-2012-02.body:
If $b \le 0$ any $n, k$ work (the left side is positive and the right side is $\le 0$), so let $b \ge 1$ and choose a prime $p > b$. Put $n = p^3$, $k = p^2$ and
$$L' = L(p^3 + 1, p^2 - 1) = \operatorname{lcm}(p^3 + 1, \ldots, p^3 + p^2 - 1).$$

**The power of $p$ in $L'$.** The multiples of $p$ among $p^3 + 1, \ldots, p^3 + p^2 - 1$ are $p^3 + jp = p(p^2 + j)$ with $1 \le j \le p - 1$; since $p \nmid p^2 + j$, each is divisible by $p$ exactly once. There is at least one ($j = 1$), so $p$ divides $L'$ exactly once.

**$L(p^3, p^2)$.** $L(p^3, p^2) = \operatorname{lcm}(p^3, L')$. The number $p^3$ has no prime factor other than $p$, so this lcm is $L'$ with the exponent of $p$ raised from $1$ to $3$: $L(p^3, p^2) = p^2L'$.

**$L(p^3 + 1, p^2)$.** $L(p^3 + 1, p^2) = \operatorname{lcm}(L', p^3 + p^2) = \operatorname{lcm}(L', p^2(p + 1))$. Among the $p^2 - 1 \ge p + 1$ consecutive integers $p^3 + 1, \ldots, p^3 + p^2 - 1$ there is a multiple of $p + 1$, so $(p + 1) \mid L'$. Hence for every prime $q \ne p$ the exponent of $q$ in $p^2(p+1)$ is at most that in $L'$, while the exponent of $p$ is $2$ versus $1$. So $L(p^3 + 1, p^2) = pL'$.

Therefore
$$L(p^3, p^2) = p^2L' = p\cdot L(p^3 + 1, p^2) > b\,L(p^3 + 1, p^2).$$
∎

cmo-cmo-2012-02.title: Factorials
cmo-cmo-2012-02.body:
Let $m \ge 3$, $n = m! - 1$, $k = m + 1$. The numbers involved in $L(n, k)$ are $m! - 1, m!, m! + 1, \ldots, m! + m - 1$.

Every one of $m!, m! + 1, \ldots, m! + m - 1$ differs from $m! - 1$ by $1, 2, \ldots, m$, so any common divisor of $m! - 1$ and one of them divides a number $\le m$, hence divides $m!$, hence divides $1$. So $m! - 1$ is coprime to all of them and
$$L(m! - 1, m + 1) = (m! - 1)\,M, \qquad M = \operatorname{lcm}(m!, m! + 1, \ldots, m! + m - 1).$$
Next $L(m!, m + 1) = \operatorname{lcm}(M, m! + m)$. Since $m! + m = m\big((m-1)! + 1\big)$ and $m \mid m! \mid M$, we get $\operatorname{lcm}(M, m! + m) \le M\big((m - 1)! + 1\big)$ (indeed $\operatorname{lcm}(M, m\cdot t)$ divides $M t$ when $m \mid M$). Therefore
$$\frac{L(m! - 1, m + 1)}{L(m!, m + 1)} \ge \frac{m! - 1}{(m-1)! + 1},$$
which tends to infinity (it exceeds $m - 2$, say, for $m \ge 3$, since $m! - 1 - (m-2)((m-1)! + 1) = 2(m-1)! - m + 1 > 0$). Choosing $m > b + 2$ gives $L(n, k) > b\,L(n + 1, k)$. ∎

cmo-cmo-2012-03.title: Two excircles coincide
cmo-cmo-2012-03.body:
Since $ABCD$ is convex, $P$ lies strictly inside both diagonals.

**The bisector of $\angle ACB$ and the bisector of $\angle APB$.** In triangle $PBC$, the angle at $C$ is $\angle PCB = \angle ACB$ (as $P$ lies on segment $CA$), so the internal bisector of $\angle ACB$ is the internal bisector of the angle $C$ of triangle $PBC$. The angle $\angle APB$ is supplementary to the angle $\angle BPC$ of triangle $PBC$, so its internal bisector is the external bisector at $P$ of triangle $PBC$. These two lines meet at the excentre $I_C$ of triangle $PBC$ opposite $C$. The corresponding excircle $\omega_C$ touches segment $PB$ and the extensions of $CP$ beyond $P$ and of $CB$ beyond $B$; the extension of $CP$ beyond $P$ is the ray $PA$. So $\omega_C$ is tangent to the two rays $PA$ and $PB$.

**Similarly** the internal bisectors of $\angle ADB$ and of $\angle APB$ meet at the excentre $I_D$ of triangle $PAD$ opposite $D$, whose excircle $\omega_D$ touches segment $PA$ and the ray $PB$ (the extension of $DP$ beyond $P$); again tangent to the rays $PA$ and $PB$.

**Tangency points.** For the excircle of triangle $PBC$ opposite $C$, let it touch line $CP$ at $Y$ and $PB$ at $X$. Tangent lengths give $CY = s$ (the semiperimeter of $PBC$), so
$$PX = PY = CY - CP = \frac{CB + BP + PC}{2} - PC = \frac{CB + BP - PC}{2}.$$
In the same way the excircle of $PAD$ opposite $D$ touches ray $PA$ at a point $X'$ with
$$PX' = \frac{DA + AP - PD}{2}.$$

**Use the hypothesis.** $AC + AD = BC + BD$ means $(AP + PC) + AD = BC + (BP + PD)$, i.e.
$$AP + AD - PD = BC + BP - PC .$$
Hence $PX = PX'$. Both $\omega_C$ and $\omega_D$ are tangent to both rays $PA$ and $PB$, and a circle tangent to both sides of the angle $APB$ is determined by the (common) distance from $P$ to its points of tangency: its centre is the point on the bisector of $\angle APB$ whose projection on $PA$ is at that distance. So $\omega_C = \omega_D$ and $I_C = I_D$.

This point lies on the bisector of $\angle ACB$, on the bisector of $\angle ADB$, and on the bisector of $\angle APB$. ∎

cmo-cmo-2012-04.title: Decrease the distance
cmo-cmo-2012-04.body:
**The passable edges connect the grid.** Let $G$ be the graph whose vertices are the squares and whose edges are the passable edges. Whenever a robot moves, it crosses an edge of $G$; so by the hypothesis (applied to any one robot) every square is joined to that robot's starting square by a walk in $G$, i.e. $G$ is connected. Conversely, for any squares $s, t$ take a path from $s$ to $t$ in $G$ and give the corresponding commands: a robot on $s$ follows this path exactly (every edge on it is passable) and arrives at $t$. So **for any two squares $s, t$ there is a command sequence moving a robot from $s$ to $t$.**

**Reduction to two robots.** Robots on the same square receive the same commands and stay together forever. So it suffices to show that any two robots can be brought to a common square: merge robot $2$ with robot $1$, then robot $3$ with that pair, and so on; at each stage the property above is all we use.

**Two robots $A$ and $B$.** For the current positions, let $d(A, B)$ be the length of a shortest command sequence that moves a robot standing on $A$'s square to $B$'s current square (it exists by the property above). If $d(A,B) = 0$ we are done. Otherwise let $S = (s_1, \ldots, s_d)$ be a shortest such sequence and apply it.

- $A$ is never blocked during $S$: if $A$ were blocked at command $s_i$, deleting $s_i$ would give a shorter sequence with the same effect on $A$.
- **Case 1: $B$ is blocked at some command $s_i$.** Let $b_0$ be $B$'s square before $S$. Skipping a command at which a robot is blocked does not change its path, so $B$ ends at the square reached from $b_0$ by the $d - 1$ commands $s_1, \ldots, s_{i-1}, s_{i+1}, \ldots, s_d$. Meanwhile $A$ ends at $b_0$. Hence now $d(A, B) \le d - 1$.
- **Case 2: $B$ is never blocked.** Then every command moves $A$ and $B$ by the same unit vector, so both are translated by the same vector $v \ne 0$ (the vector from $A$'s square to $b_0$). Now $A$ is at $b_0$ and $B$ at $b_0 + v$. A robot at $b_0$ that receives $S$ moves exactly as $B$ just did, so $S$ still takes $A$ to $B$ and $d(A, B) \le d$. If $d(A,B) < d$ we have made progress; otherwise $S$ is again a shortest sequence and we apply it again.

If Case 2 occurred $m$ times in a row, $B$ would have been translated by $mv$; as the grid is finite and $v \neq 0$, this is impossible for large $m$. Hence after finitely many applications of $S$, $d(A, B)$ strictly decreases.

Since $d(A, B)$ is a non-negative integer, after finitely many rounds $d(A, B) = 0$: the two robots share a square. By the reduction, all robots can be gathered on one square. ∎

cmo-cmo-2012-05.title: Count selections of each volume
cmo-cmo-2012-05.body:
Let $t_k$ be the number of times volume $k$ is selected.

**When does the process stop?** Only when no volume is too far right, i.e. every volume $k$ is in a position $\le k$. Then volume $1$ is in position $1$, volume $2$ in a position $\le 2$ other than $1$, i.e. $2$, and so on: the order is correct.

**Key claim.** Between two consecutive selections of volume $k$, some volume with label $< k$ is selected.

*Proof.* Right after volume $k$ is selected it is in position $k$. Suppose that afterwards only volumes with labels $> k$ are selected. A move of volume $j > k$ removes it from a position $p > j$ and inserts it at position $j$. If $k$ is at position $q \le k$, then $q < j < p$: removing a volume to the right of $k$ and inserting it to the right of $k$ (at position $j > q$) leaves $k$ at position $q$. So $k$ stays in a position $\le k$, is never too far right, and cannot be selected again. $\square$

Hence $t_k \le 1 + (t_1 + \cdots + t_{k-1})$. In particular $t_1 \le 1$, and by induction $t_k \le 1 + (1 + 2 + \cdots + 2^{k-2}) = 2^{k-1}$. Also $t_n = 0$, because volume $n$ is never in a position $> n$.

**(a)** The total number of steps is
$$t_1 + \cdots + t_{n-1} \le 1 + 2 + \cdots + 2^{n-2} = 2^{n-1} - 1,$$
so the process terminates, and (as shown above) it terminates exactly when the books are in order.

**(b) The bound $2^{n-1}-1$ is attained.** Use the rule "always select the **rightmost** volume that is too far right".

**Lemma.** Let $k \ge 1$ and suppose the last $k + 1$ positions $p, p+1, \ldots, p+k$ of the shelf (so $p + k = n$) hold the volumes
$$y,\ p,\ p+1,\ \ldots,\ p+k-1$$
in this order ($y$ is any volume; each of $p, \ldots, p+k-1$ is exactly one place too far right). Then after exactly $2^k - 1$ steps of the rule these positions hold $p, p+1, \ldots, p+k-1, y$; every selected volume is one of $p, \ldots, p+k-1$, and the positions $< p$ are never touched.

*Proof by induction on $k$.* Every insertion happens at a position equal to the label of the selected volume, which is $\ge p$; so positions $< p$ are untouched once we know only volumes $p, \ldots, p+k-1$ are selected. Also, since our positions are the last ones on the shelf, "rightmost eligible volume of the shelf" is the same as "rightmost eligible volume among positions $\ge p$" whenever one of the latter is eligible.

- $k = 1$: positions $p, p+1$ hold $y, p$. Volume $p$ (last position) is eligible; moving it to position $p$ gives $p, y$. One step $= 2^1 - 1$.
- $k \ge 2$: positions $p+1, \ldots, p+k$ hold $p, p+1, \ldots, p+k-1$, which is the configuration of the lemma for $k - 1$ (with $p+1$ in place of $p$ and the volume $p$ in the role of $y$). By the induction hypothesis, after $2^{k-1} - 1$ steps, all selecting volumes among $p+1, \ldots, p+k-1$, the last $k+1$ positions hold $y, p+1, \ldots, p+k-1, p$. Now $p+1, \ldots, p+k-1$ are in their correct places and volume $p$, in position $p + k$, is the rightmost eligible volume; it is moved to position $p$, giving $p, y, p+1, \ldots, p+k-1$. The last $k$ positions now hold $y, p+1, \ldots, p+k-1$ — again the configuration for $k-1$ — and by the induction hypothesis $2^{k-1} - 1$ further steps turn them into $p+1, \ldots, p+k-1, y$. In total $(2^{k-1} - 1) + 1 + (2^{k-1} - 1) = 2^k - 1$ steps. $\square$

Apply the lemma to the starting order $(n, 1, 2, \ldots, n-1)$ with $p = 1$, $k = n - 1$, $y = n$: the process takes exactly $2^{n-1} - 1$ steps before reaching $1, 2, \ldots, n$. (For $n = 3$: $312 \to 321 \to 132 \to 123$.) Together with (a), the maximum is $2^{n-1} - 1$.

**Answer: (b) $2^{n-1} - 1$.** ∎
